lead: Today we remember the first church built in the name of the holy Mother of God, and the Gospel speaks of true worship: “the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth.” Paul, writing to Corinth, tells each believer to remain with God in the condition in which God called them, since what counts is “obeying the commandments of God”. Both readings ask where God is truly found and served. The key words are calling and worship.

r.h: Remain with God where you were called
set: In chapter 7 Paul answers questions the Corinthians had sent him: “Now concerning the matters about which you wrote” (7:1). Some thought that becoming a Christian meant changing everything at once: leaving marriage, changing one's social state, undoing one's past. In the middle of his answers about marriage Paul gives a general rule and illustrates it with two examples: circumcision and slavery.
str: v. 17: the rule: live the life to which God called you.
vv. 18–19: circumcised or uncircumcised: what matters is keeping God's commandments.
vv. 20–23: slave or not: in the Lord the slave is the Lord's freed person, and every Christian belongs to Christ.
v. 24: remain with God in your calling.
kw: For Paul the “calling” is first God's call to faith and to belong to Christ. Our outward condition is the place where we answer that call; it is not the call itself.
“You were bought with a price” (7:23; also 6:20). The price is the blood of Christ. Those who have been bought by him cannot again sell themselves to any human master.
vv: let each of you lead the life that the Lord has assigned, to which God called you.
Paul says this is his rule “in all the churches”. Holiness does not wait for perfect circumstances; it begins where God finds us.
Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing; but obeying the commandments of God is everything.

A striking sentence from a Jew who had been circumcised on the eighth day (Philippians 3:5). Paul does not despise his heritage; he says that what saves is God's grace received in faith and lived in obedience.
Even if you can gain your freedom, make use of your present condition now more than ever.

The Greek of the second half is brief and can be read two ways: “make use of your present condition” (NRSV text) or “avail yourself of the opportunity” (NRSV note). The POC takes the second: if you can gain your freedom, use the chance. Either way, Paul does not praise slavery.
In whatever condition you were called, brothers and sisters, there remain with God.
The last words, “with God”, are the key. Whatever our state of life, the real question is whether we remain in his presence.
ch: The Church reads this passage as a teaching on vocation: every state of life, married or single, rich or poor, can become the place of holiness (Lumen Gentium 41). Paul's words about slaves are not a defence of slavery. In his letter to Philemon he asks a master to receive his slave back “no longer as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother” (Philemon 16), and the Church teaches plainly that enslaving human beings is a sin against their dignity (CCC 2414). Paul's point is that no human condition can stand between a person and the call of Christ.

set: Jesus is resting at Jacob's well near the Samaritan town of Sychar. He has asked a Samaritan woman for a drink, crossing two boundaries at once, since “Jews do not share things in common with Samaritans” (4:9). As the conversation deepens, she raises the old question that divided the two peoples: “Our ancestors worshiped on this mountain, but you say that the place where people must worship is in Jerusalem” (4:20).

The mountain is Gerizim. The Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses and had built a temple on Gerizim, which was destroyed by the Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus in the late second century BC. Jesus' answer moves the question from the place of worship to the person in whom God is worshipped.
str: v. 21: neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.
v. 22: salvation is from the Jews.
vv. 23–24: true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth.
vv. 25–26: the woman speaks of the Messiah; Jesus says, “I am he.”
kw: The word first meant to bow down in reverence. It comes again and again in these verses: the whole conversation is about worship.
Not simply “sincerely” or “inwardly”. In John, the Spirit is the Holy Spirit whom Jesus will give, and the Truth is Jesus himself (14:6). True worship is worship in the Spirit, through Christ.

Literally “I am”. In John this phrase often recalls the name God revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14). Here it is the first time in the Gospel that Jesus openly says who he is, and he says it to a Samaritan woman.
vv: Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.
“Woman” is not a cold word in John; Jesus uses it also for his mother (2:4; 19:26). The “hour” in John is the hour of his death and glorification. From the cross a new worship will begin.
for salvation is from the Jews.
Jesus does not set aside Israel's faith; he affirms it. The Messiah comes from Israel, and the Church never forgets this root (CCC 528; Nostra Aetate 4).
But the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth,
“And is now here”: because Jesus is present, the new worship has already begun. The Father himself “seeks” such worshippers; worship begins with God's desire for us.
I am he, the one who is speaking to you.
The woman had placed the Messiah in the future. Jesus places him in the present, in front of her. She will leave her water jar and become a witness to her town (4:28–29).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the worship “in Spirit and in truth” of the New Covenant is not tied exclusively to any one place, because the whole earth is sacred and entrusted to the children of men. Yet when believers gather, they are the living stones built into a spiritual house, and so, where religious liberty allows, Christians build churches as visible signs of the Church living in that place (CCC 1179–1180). Churches dedicated to the Mother of God belong to this picture. The Council of Ephesus in 431 confessed Mary as Theotokos, Mother of God, because the one she bore is truly God; a church in her name is a confession of faith in her Son.

qa: If true worship is “in spirit and truth”, do we still need church buildings?

Yes. Jesus does not abolish places of prayer; he himself went up to the Temple for the feasts. He says that worship is no longer bound to one mountain or one city, because it is offered in him and through the Spirit. A church is the house where the Church, the people of God, gathers for that worship, above all for the Holy Qurbono (CCC 1180–1181). The building serves the living temple; it does not replace it.
rite: Our calendar keeps today the memory of the founding of the first church in the name of the holy Mother of God. It does not say where or when that church was built, and we need not supply what it does not say. What it asks us to remember is that, very early, the disciples of Jesus gave houses of prayer the name of his Mother. In the Syriac tradition she is called Yoldath Aloho, the one who gave birth to God, and many of our parishes bear her name. Each such church is a sign that Christians come to the Son in the company of his Mother.
study: Paul tells me to remain with God in the condition in which I was called. Am I waiting for better circumstances before I try to be holy?
Jesus says the Father seeks true worshippers. How do I prepare to worship in spirit and truth when I come to the Holy Qurbono?
